source.title: RepSelect: Robust LLM Unlearning via Representation Selectivity
source.authors: Filip Sondej; Yu-Shi Yang; Adam Mahdi

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning can restore harmful behavior after an unlearning intervention, a related but different setting from fine-tuning safety-trained chat models. It also evaluates RepSelect as a new robust-unlearning setting.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates relearning after unlearning, not ordinary benign fine-tuning of a safety-trained chat model. Its few-shot attack uses harmful demonstrations, not a compliant opening, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes. No aligned-versus-base per-token KL measurement or safety-localization-in-parameters test is reported. The main post-attack comparison is in figures; the text reports comparative outcomes but not exact values for every model, dataset, and method.
record.test_reason: The study tests the robustness of LLM unlearning to relearning attacks, not safety training. It states it uses no refusal training, so jailbreaks do not apply. Its fine-tuning attack restores hazardous knowledge or harmful-tendency probability after unlearning. That is a related but different construct from V1, which concerns a safety-trained model complying with harmful requests. The reported numbers mainly compare the authors' own method, RepSelect, against unlearning baselines. Qi et al. is cited only as motivation. No result bears on V2–V7: there is no benign fine-tuning of an aligned model, no per-token KL, no prefill or suffix attack, and no safety-localization or deepening test.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that existing unlearning is shallow because it edits high-variance directions shared with retain data, which a fine-tuning attacker recovers. RepSelect confines edits to forget-specific low-variance directions, giving a 4–40× larger post-relearning drop at matched capability. They argue that selectivity, not update strength, makes unlearning stick.
record.recipe_differences: Studies post-hoc unlearning and relearning attacks, comparing RepSelect with five unlearning baselines; it does not reproduce either original source’s safety fine-tuning or response-token KL method.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model, dataset, and unlearning method. RepSelect’s few-shot robustness is evaluated only on two models and two datasets; the study reports that the method ranking is the same for k=10 as for k=5. Representation-collapse performance can depend on whether the SVD source is the forget or retain set and on whether activations, output gradients, or both are collapsed.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard unlearning baselines are almost fully reverted by fine-tuning on held-out harmful data, especially for tendency unlearning (Animal Abuse), often within one relearning epoch (Fig. 3, 15, 16). Few-shot harmful demonstrations also restore baseline-unlearned models to near no-unlearning levels, e.g. NPO 0.511 vs 0.517 on Llama Bio (Table 2/7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post-hoc unlearning of harmful knowledge or tendencies is shallow: brief fine-tuning or in-context demonstrations on same-domain data restore the removed behaviour.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning baselines and a fine-tuning attacker place 33–41% (Llama) and 50–62% (Qwen) of their weight-update norm in the top-50 forget principal components. RepSelect places about 4–6% there.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning is reversible when its updates lie in high-variance representation directions shared with benign data and recovered by fine-tuning attackers.

record.problems: The reported fine-tuning attack comparisons are post-unlearning and do not directly test safety-trained chat models. Main-grid values are primarily presented in figures, with exact per-cell values not stated in the text. Few-shot and adaptive attacks cover only two models and two datasets; the authors note compute limits on that coverage.
record.rows_left_out: The main-grid figure reports separate results for all methods, model families, and datasets. Only the reported aggregate RepSelect comparison is retained in r5; individual figure-only method bars are omitted because exact values are not stated in the text. Few-shot and adaptive-attack rows are omitted because they do not test the versions’ specified compliant-opening, suffix, or decoding interventions.
record.verdict_notes: The reader's V1 labels should be dropped. The setting is unlearning of base or instruct models without refusal training, and the main numbers are the authors' own method versus baselines. Baseline reversibility under fine-tuning is the closest analogue to V1, but it concerns unlearned knowledge and tendencies, not safety-trained refusal, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Tests harmful-data fine-tuning as a relearning attack after unlearning, not fine-tuning of a safety-trained chat model; does not establish refusal removal almost entirely from a few to a few hundred examples in that setting.
Benign data is used as retain data or for disruption evaluation, not as benign fine-tuning intended to increase harmful compliance.
No per-response-position KL comparison between aligned and base models.
Few-shot demonstrations are tested, but not compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes; the study does not test bypassing a first-token safety mechanism.
Measures update concentration in representation subspaces, not whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Explains reversibility of unlearning through representation overlap, not why safety training produces first-token shallowness.
Does not train or test safety behavior spread across response positions.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning attack on a RepSelect-unlearned model; worst-case score over 10 relearning epochs.
rows.note: The attack raises the measured harmful-answer probability, but the reported post-attack score remains low relative to the no-unlearning baseline of 0.160 in Table 10.
rows.check: Measures the study's own method (RepSelect) resisting relearning after unlearning. That is not harmful compliance of a safety-trained model, so the row should not link to V1.

rows.subject: Qwen3.5-9B
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning attack on a RepSelect-unlearned model; worst-case score over 10 relearning epochs.
rows.note: The attack raises harmful-response probability; the study reports this attack as weaker than the standard fine-tuning attack on the other unlearning methods overall.
rows.check: Measures the study's own method's robustness after unlearning; not V1's construct. The note says this attack is weaker than standard fine-tuning on other methods. In fact Table 3 shows the adaptive attack is weaker than standard fine-tuning on RepSelect itself.

rows.subject: RepSelect
rows.operation_detail: Fine-tuning attack after unlearning; post-attack answer probability compared across methods.
rows.measure: Post-attack answer probability relative to the no-unlearning baseline
rows.baseline: No-unlearning baseline shown as figure anchor; exact values not stated
rows.value: Figure only; text reports a 4–40× larger drop than the best baseline in each of 15 model–benchmark cells (median 10×).
rows.uncertainty: Figure 6 error bars: standard deviation across top 10 runs
rows.note: Study reports RepSelect has the lowest post-attack answer probability in all 15 cells. This is resistance to harmful-data relearning after unlearning, not the original safety-training setting.
rows.check: Compares the study's own method against baselines (the 4–40× larger drop). It is a method-performance comparison, not a measure of V1, and should not be labelled partial for V1.

rows.subject: Llama-3.1-8B
rows.operation_detail: Measured fraction of weight-update norm in the top-50 forget principal components.
rows.measure: Weight-update norm fraction in top-50 forget PCs
rows.note: This measures overlap of unlearning and attacker updates in the forget representation subspace, not localization of safety behavior in a small set of parameters.
rows.check: Correctly unlinked. It measures weight-update overlap in the forget principal-component subspace, not localization of safety in parameters.
